title: Batch-triggered scale misprediction (cold-prefix suppression) — postmortem
creator: Priya Patel
description:
Summary:
During a production capacity event on 2025-02-17 02:10–03:40 UTC, several customer routes experienced sustained latency increases and 20–40% request errors as worker pools failed to scale fast enough for incoming traffic bursts. Root cause analysis shows a regression in how our KEDA-based scaler sampled queue metrics in the presence of larger intra-request batching windows and cold-prefix behavior: requests were being held by the batching layer long enough that the external queue metric (queue_length) undershot the true incoming rate, producing false negative scale decisions and underprovisioning.

Impact:
- Affected services: hosted inference for small-model tier in us-west-2 across two Dedicated clusters.
- User impact: increased request latency (p95 from 120ms to 860ms) and elevated 5xx rates (peak 32% on impacted routes).
- Duration: 90 minutes of sustained degradation, with partial recovery after manual threshold adjustments and a temporary probe injection.

Timeline (UTC):
- 02:08: Sensors detect 4x normal arrival rate to a small-model pool.
- 02:10: Latency and 5xx begin to climb; initial autoscale decisions do not trigger additional replica creation.
- 02:25: On-call notices anomaly; first mitigation attempts are manual (increase KEDA min replicas).
- 02:40: We deploy a short-lived synthetic probe (15s steady traffic) to force scale-up; latency begins to fall.
- 03:35: Flow returns to baseline as autoscaler thresholds adjusted and backlog drains.

Root cause analysis:
1) Metric distortion by batching: Our serving runtime introduced a larger batching window (micro-optimization change deployed 2025-01-29) which decreased instantaneous queue length visibility. Requests were buffered inside the runtime until a batching threshold or a timeout, so KEDA's external scaler saw fewer items in the work queue than were actually arriving.
2) Cold-prefix warmup behavior: Many bursts contained prefixes requiring KV-cache/warmup work, which increased per-request tail latency while still holding requests in the local buffer. This masked the true system load from the external scaler.
3) Sampling cadence mismatch: KEDA scaler used a short metric scrape window tuned for immediate queue spikes; with buffering and warmup, the metric signal was smoothed below the alerting threshold.
4) Regression vector: The batching window change was intended to improve throughput and token efficiency but lacked a compensating change to autoscaling observability (no prefix-warmup metric exported and no synthetic probe configured).

Evidence:
- Dashboard: internal/dashboard/autoscale/us-west-2/small-model (link: https://dash.redwood.ai/board/USW2/SMALL/428199) shows queue_length metric at 0–2 while latency and inflight requests spiked.
- Traces: Distributed traces indicate increased span time in runtime/batching and kv_warmup spans.
- Deployment diff: runtime PR #8421 increased batching window default from 12ms to 40ms (https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8421).

Immediate mitigations performed:
- Reverted KEDA minReplica increase back to baseline once traffic normalized.
- Deployed a temporary synthetic probe (15s pacing) that bypassed batching and exercised the real worker queue so the scaler saw true demand.
- Rolled back the most aggressive batching timeout on two smallest pools as hotfix.

Lessons learned:
- Batching optimizations can hide demand signals from external scalers — autoscaler inputs must be resilient to buffering layers.
- We lack a targeted metric that quantifies prefix-warmup cost and buffered request backlog.
- Synthetic probes (control-plane generated) are an effective short-term lever and should be part of our runbook.

Action items (owners and due dates):
1) Export a prefix_warmup metric from the runtime and add it to the autoscaling metric set (owner: Marco Alvarez; due: 2025-03-07).
2) Add a buffered_queue_length metric representing requests currently held in runtime buffers (owner: Saira Khan; due: 2025-03-10).
3) Update KEDA scaler configuration to consider a composite metric (queue_length + buffered_queue_length + prefix_warmup) and tune thresholds for smoothing effects (owner: Backend Autoscale Team; due: 2025-03-17).
4) Implement control-plane synthetic probes ability to target specific pools and prefixes (owner: Platform Team - Rafael Ortega; due: 2025-04-01).
5) Add e2e chaos test that simulates batching + KV warmup bursts against the autoscaler in staging (owner: Reliability QA - Lena Fischer; due: 2025-03-21).
6) Roll back and add guardrail to any batching window change: require autoscaler impact assessment and metric export before rollout (owner: Runtime PM - Priya Patel; due: 2025-03-05).
7) Document runbook step: how to inject a synthetic probe and temporary config knobs for fast mitigation (owner: On-call docs - Jordan Lee; due: 2025-02-28).

Verification plan:
- Staging validation: run the chaos test 5x with varied burst sizes and validate that composite metric triggers scale-up within target SLO (owner: Reliability QA; verify by 2025-03-25).
- Canary: deploy buffered_queue_length export and composite scaler in canary region for two weeks, monitor p95 and scale events (owner: Backend Autoscale Team; canary start 2025-03-29).
- Dashboard additions: add a combined-signal panel and an automated alert when combined signal exceeds threshold but queue_length alone does not (owner: Observability - Mei Tan; due: 2025-03-12).

Follow-ups and gating:
- Block deploys that change batching windows without a signed autoscaler impact note (enforce in release checklist).
- Coordinate with customer success for targeted customers who experienced the incident for post-incident outreach (owner: CS - Ayesha Kapoor; due: 2025-03-07).

Artifacts and links:
- Runtime batching PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8421
- Incident dashboard: https://dash.redwood.ai/board/USW2/SMALL/428199
- Runbook draft (internal): https://docs.redwood.ai/runbooks/autoscale-synthetic-probe
- Hotfix PR (rollback): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8479

Conclusion:
This incident exposed a blind spot where internal buffering improved token efficiency but masked incoming load from our external autoscaler, producing false negative scale decisions during bursts that included cold-prefix work. The remediation plan focuses on increasing observability (buffer and warmup metrics), making the autoscaler composite-aware, and preventing similar regressions via deploy guardrails and tests. The immediate hotfixes restored availability; the medium-term work will reduce the chance of recurrence and make scale signals robust to buffering layers.
